title: The system: ad-click analytics that counts once on ingest and reconciles nightly
caption: A streaming job folds clicks into minute rows as they arrive; the raw archive is the source of truth that a nightly batch uses to correct and finalise the numbers.

steps.text: Ad servers emit one event per click (event id, ad id, timestamp, price) to a stream partitioned by ad id: about 40 000 events/s at peak.
The stream processor keeps an open one-minute window per active ad in memory and, when the window closes, upserts an (ad, minute) row with count and spend.
Hour and day rows are built from the minute rows, and each tier is kept for longer: 30 days, 1 year, forever.
The same events are archived untouched in hourly files: the raw archive is the source of truth, and analysts query it through the warehouse.
Every night a batch job recomputes yesterday from raw (dedup by event id, invalid-click filtering), overwrites the hour and day rows, and sends final spend to billing.
A dashboard asks for 'clicks per hour, last 7 days, my campaign'. The query API checks ownership, picks the hour tier and reads 168 rows per ad.

scenarios.name: Traffic spike
scenarios.summary: A live sports final brings 8× the usual clicks. The stream buffers, the processor lags a little, and dashboards stay fast.

steps.text: The stream absorbs the burst; processors scale out up to one per partition and lag by about a minute.
Rollup write volume grows with active ads, not with clicks: one row per ad per minute either way.
Dashboard queries are unchanged in cost; they show 'data as of 12:41' so the lag is visible, not hidden.

scenarios.name: Processor crash
scenarios.summary: A processor dies with open windows in memory. It restarts from a checkpoint and replays; rows are written as absolute values, so nothing is double counted.

steps.text: One processor instance dies; its open windows for 2 000 ads vanish from memory.
A replacement loads the last checkpoint (window state plus stream offsets, taken every 30 s) and replays the stream from there.
It rewrites the same (ad, minute) rows with the full value (set, not increment), so replayed events don't add twice.
Nightly recon from raw would correct any drift anyway.

scenarios.name: Fraud rule change
scenarios.summary: The fraud team tightens the invalid-click rule. Streaming numbers keep the old rule for today; recon restates the past from raw.

steps.text: A new rule ships to the batch job first; the streaming job gets it on its next deploy.
Tonight's recon recomputes yesterday with the new rule and overwrites the hour and day rows.
A backfill reruns recon for the last 30 days, oldest day first; billing gets corrected totals and a credit note.
Dashboards label days as 'final' or 'provisional', so a changed number is explained, not a surprise.
